event.title: Big Earth Hackathon: Wildland Fire Challenge
event.description:
Big Earth Hackathon: Wildland Fire Challenge bridges the gap between innovation and impact by bringing Stanford students together with real-world stakeholders to design, build, and prototype solutions to one of today’s most pressing global systems crises — wildfire.

Big Earth Hackathon is a 9 week challenge and optional companion course launching fall quarter at Stanford, open to undergraduates, graduate students, and postdocs across all disciplines at Stanford. Teams will tackle some of the most pressing wildfire challenges – from early detection and suppression, to fuel management, to community prevention – developing technology solutions using a user-centered design approach. Teams hear directly from practitioners and stakeholders who define the needs, and are supported by technical workshops throughout the quarter.

event.title: For the Next Generation: Mental Health in Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Youth
event.address: Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity (CCSRE), 450 Jane Stanford Way Building 360, Stanford, CA 94305
tags: Asian American Research Center at Stanford
event.description:
Join the Asian American Research Center at Stanford (AARCS) for this free public event to launch a new book, "For the Next Generation". This new edited volume brings together the latest scholarship on mental health among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander (AANHPI) youth and addresses how research can be applied to clinical practice.

This panel will include presentations and discussions with contributors to the edited volume, clinicians, and community leaders who will cover topics such as ethnic-racial identity development, ideal affect, and neurodiversity. The discussions will emphasize how we can ensure that evidence-based interventions for AANHPIs are culturally responsive, guided by community perspectives, and integrated with creative, non-traditional approaches. This gathering is for clinicians, researchers, educators, and community leaders who are interested in applying the latest research evidence to direct clinical and creative applications to improve the mental health and well-being of AANHPI youth and young adult populations.

Panelists:

  • Dr. Janie Hong, Clinical Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University

  • Dr. Helen Hsu, Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences and Director of Outreach for Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS), Vaden Health Services, Stanford University

  • Dr. Nancy Liu, Professor of Psychology, University of California Berkeley

  • Elaine Peng, Founder and Executive Director of Mental Health Association for Chinese Communities (NAMI Chinese)

  • Dr. Jeanne Tsai, Dunlevie Family Professor, Professor of Psychology, Stanford University

  • Dr. Tiffany Yip, Professor of Psychology, Fordham University

 

Please contact Laureen Hom (redacted@stanford.edu) if you have any questions

Co-sponsored by the Asian American Activities Center (A3C) and Asian American Studies Program

event.title: Hospice 101
event.description:
Hospice has been part of the medical system in the US since the mid-1970s, yet there is still so much misinformation and misunderstanding about hospice and its role in providing the best possible care at the end of life.

Join us for this free webinar to debunk the myths about hospice and have your questions answered. You will learn what hospice is, why you might want hospice care for yourself or a loved one, when to start thinking about moving to hospice, and how to request it if you no longer want aggressive treatments and tests in the hospital. You will also learn how to cover the costs of hospice care, which is often covered at no cost through your Medicare contributions.

There will be time allowed for questions and resources will be provided, so you will leave the session better informed on this compassionate choice for end-of-life care.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants.

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.

Request disability accommodations and access info.

Class details are subject to change.

event.title: View From The Top: Channing Dungey, Chairman and CEO of Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD U.S. Networks
event.description:
Highly esteemed entertainment industry leader Channing Dungey serves as Chairman and CEO of Warner Bros. Television Group and Warner Bros. Discovery’s US Networks. She was tapped to run the Television Group in October 2020 and began her tenure in January 2021. In this role, she has creative responsibility for all of Warner Bros.’ unrivaled television production activities, including live-action scripted series, unscripted programming, and animation. She is the first woman and first Black executive to run WBTVG. In January 2025, Dungey’s remit expanded to include oversight of WBD’s US Networks business.

As head of WBTVG, Dungey oversees Warner Bros. Television, the Studio’s flagship television production unit for live-action scripted programming, as well as unscripted programming produced by its Warner Horizon Unscripted Television, Telepictures, and Shed Media labels. Dungey also has oversight of animated production from Warner Bros. Animation, Cartoon Network Studios, and Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe.

As of August 2026, WBTVG’s divisions are producing more than 80 projects for over 20 platforms, including Warner Bros. Discovery’s HBO, HBO Max, and US Networks, external streaming services, the broadcast networks, cable channels, and local stations.

As head of the US Networks, Dungey oversees WBD’s premier linear TV business. The renowned brands which make up this portfolio include Discovery, Food Network, HGTV, Investigation Discovery, Magnolia Network, TLC, Adult Swim, Cartoon Network, OWN, TBS, TNT, and truTV.

Prior to joining Warner Bros., Dungey served as Vice President of Original Series at Netflix. Before that, Dungey served as president of ABC Entertainment, the first Black executive to run a major television network. In that role, she oversaw all development, programming, marketing, and scheduling operations for ABC primetime and late-night.

Her career in entertainment spans both television and film. She partnered with Pamela Post and formed Dexterity Pictures, a production partnership focused on making both studio and independent films, as well as developing television series. She also served as president of Material, a film production company with a first-look deal at Warner Bros. Prior to that, she served for five years as a Warner Bros. production executive, helping to develop and supervise a diverse range of commercially successful, critically acclaimed films.

Dungey has received many nominations and awards in recognition of her career accomplishments, including being honored with the Brandon Tartikoff Legacy Award, presented by NATPE (National Association of Television Program Executives) in 2022. She was also recognized by Varietyas one of its Power of Women: Los Angeles honorees in 2021, and she was named Television Executive of the Year by Adweek in 2024. In 2026, she was named a USA Today Women of the Year National Honoree.

event.title: ESE Seminar - Bo Guo: "Fate and Transport of PFAS in Unsaturated Porous Media across Scales:   Interfacial Partitioning, Thin Water Films, and Upscaling"
event.description:
Abstract

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are contaminants that have accumulated extensively in soils, which can act as long-term sources of groundwater contamination. Quantifying soil PFAS leaching is therefore critical for risk assessment, remediation, and regulatory decision-making. However, PFAS transport differs fundamentally from that of conventional contaminants because many PFAS are surfactants that adsorb at air–water and solid–water interfaces, leading to complex retention behavior and flow–transport coupling under variably saturated conditions.

I present a cross-scale framework for understanding and modeling PFAS fate and transport in soils and groundwater. I discuss the dominant processes controlling PFAS retention and migration, introduce a mechanistic mathematical model that incorporates PFAS-specific interfacial processes, and show how thin water films can uniquely control PFAS transport in unsaturated soils. This is followed by a multi-continuum, semi-analytical framework as a potential route for upscaling these processes and incorporating them into practical modeling tools. The goal is to connect interfacial physics across scales to improve predictions of long-term PFAS retention, leaching, and mass discharge to groundwater.

Bio

Dr. Bo Guo is an Associate Professor and University Distinguished Scholar at the University of Arizona. His research focuses on fluid flow and transport in porous media, with an emphasis on multiscale mathematical and computational modeling. He works on a range of environmental and energy problems, including contaminant transport in soils and groundwater, chemical weathering in the critical zone, shale oil and gas production, and geologic carbon storage. Bo earned his B.S. (with highest honor) from Tsinghua University and Ph.D. from Princeton University, and completed a two-year postdoc at Stanford University before joining the University of Arizona. He is the 2027 Henry Darcy Distinguished Lecturer, and a recipient of the AGU Hydrologic Sciences Early Career Award, NSF CAREER Award, and the Humboldt Research Fellowship for Experienced Researchers. He serves as an Editor of Hydrology and Earth System Sciences and an Associate Editor of Water Resources Research, and Advances in Water Resources.

Daniel Wurgaft | A Resource Rational Analysis of Representations: Geometry, Inference, Capacity
event.room_number: James Lin and Nisa Leung Seminar Room, E153
event.description:
Abstract

Neural systems process information by forming representations of the world. Studies of representational geometry have revealed remarkably structured representations in biological and artificial systems, as well as surprising alignment in representations across systems. Why do representations across systems converge to similar structures, how do these structures encode concepts and uncertainty over them, and how are they shaped by resource constraints?

Here, we tackle these questions in neural networks through the lens of resource rationality, asking what representations are optimal for solving a task, given dimensionality and linear readout constraints. We derive a notion of optimal linear representations, and show that these emerge across varied architectures and tasks, providing a simple explanation for representational convergence as alignment toward the optimal solution. This shared treatment motivates a normative formalization of conceptual spaces that generalizes the linear representation hypothesis. We then extend this account to uncertainty and inference over conceptual spaces, asking how representations should change in response to in-context evidence, and finally to resource-constrained settings involving representational interference.


About the Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series 

The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share  insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science. 

As neuroscience continues to generate vast amounts of data—from intricate neural circuit maps to large-scale brain activity recordings—the need for interdisciplinary expertise in data science, statistics, and engineering has never been more critical. 

The Center for Neural Data Science mission is to advance brain research through the development of cutting-edge analytical methodologies and collaborative approaches. Stanford's affiliates are invited to join this vibrant community dedicated to transformative discoveries.

This seminar series is only offered in person.

event.title: HAI & AI Governance Lab | A Conversation with Jacob Coxon & Rob Reich
event.description:
This in-person event is open to current Stanford faculty, students, and staff. ID will be required at check in. Other guests are invited to join the webinar.

The companies building artificial intelligence have promised to transform the world. But who gets to decide what that transformation looks like and what happens when people who have worked inside those companies question their direction? Jacob Coxon recently made a very public decision to leave Anthropic, a company that has made the responsible development of AI central to its identity. His departure opens a window into a greater debate about technological ambition, institutional accountability, and the responsibilities of the companies building these increasingly powerful systems. In this conversation, Coxon will join Stanford Professor Rob Reich to discuss his departure from Anthropic and the questions it raises about safety, power, and principles in the AI industry.

Space is limited; registration is available first-come, first served.

event.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | More Value per Tonne: Rethinking How We Use Rock | Tiziana Vanorio, Stanford University
event.description:
Rocks may seem ordinary and ubiquitous, but they are the foundation of the geomaterials that underpin modern society—from cement in our built environment to the critical minerals in our smartphones and energy technologies. As the energy transition accelerates and demand for physical infrastructure grows, demand for materials is increasing rapidly. Simply extracting more resources to meet this demand is costly and environmentally consequential. Decades of innovation have made cars more fuel-efficient and batteries more effective; can we apply the same principle to Earth materials? Just as fuel efficiency asks how far we can go on a gallon of fuel, resource efficiency asks how much value we can obtain from a tonne of rock. Rocks themselves may be inexpensive, but extracting, processing, transporting, and developing or expanding the resource are not. Improving material retention and quarry utilization efficiency can therefore create more value from the resources we already extract.

This seminar explores three ways to make each tonne of rock more productive: retaining more usable material through feedstock redesign, extracting multiple values through water–rock interactions, and selecting better through smart sensing. Specifically, we will examine how feedstock redesign for cement can enable lower-temperature processing and decarbonization while conserving mass, increasing material yield and retention; how water interacting with rock under thermal and chemical gradients can mobilize valuable elements and create additional value streams; and how smart sensing could support more targeted extraction by revealing where valuable properties occur within heterogeneous rock resources. Ultimately, resource efficiency asks us to shift the question from how much we can extract to how much useful value we can obtain from what we extract.

Tiziana Vanorio, is a Professor of Geophysics in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford University, with a courtesy appointment in Civil and Environmental Engineering. She leads the Rock Physics and Geomaterials Laboratory, where her research investigates the physics of Earth materials and how their properties evolve through fluid interactions and mechanical and chemical transformations across scales. Her group integrates laboratory experiments, rock physics, and multiscale characterization to connect mineral and microstructural processes to the behavior of rocks and geomaterials. This understanding is used to engineer the subsurface and develop resource-efficient materials, including applications in geothermal systems, CO₂ mineralization, critical minerals, and new cementitious materials inspired by natural mineral transformation and cementation. 

Seminar background

The Stanford Energy Seminar delivers a wide variety of perspectives on energy to the Stanford community, including academics, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and executives with utilities and non-profits. The series has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. 

Anyone with an interest in energy is welcome to join! You can enjoy seminars in the following ways:

  • Attend live. The auditorium may change quarter by quarter, so check each seminar event to confirm the location. Explore the current quarter's schedule.
  • Watch live in a browser livestream if available. Check each seminar event for its unique livestream URL.
  • Watch recordings of past seminars 
    • Available on the Past Energy Seminars page and the Energy Seminars playlist of the Stanford Energy YouTube channel
  • (For students) Take the seminar as a 1-unit class (CEE 301/ENERGY 301/MS&E 494)

event.title: Tim Bakken, Professor of Law, U.S. Military Academy, West Point on The Consequences of Silence When Academic Freedom and Expression are at Risk: Learning to Speak and Act According to Your Conscience
event.description: This presentation will describe Mr. Bakken’s personal experience as well as a broader overview of the dynamics within universities when students, staff, faculty, and members of other institutions express dissenting opinions, and, as a result, experience adverse treatment (e.g., out casting). It is posited that supporters of dissenters or their viewpoints will remain silent, unable to offer assistance, unless institutions teach that the content of expression is not a basis on which to punish or isolate people. Time will be allotted to discuss the relevance of these issues within Stanford University.

event.title: War, Sanctions and the Intimacy of Everyday Life
event.description:
In this panel conversation, Negar Mottahedeh and Salar Mameni discuss themes of war, loss, sanctions and the possibility of love and intimacy with Iranians from the position of exile in the diaspora. 

Negar Mottahedeh will read a text titled “How My Instagram Hacker Changed My Life,” a tale that begins with the theft of her Instagram handle and follows the unlikely friendship that emerged between her, an Iranian professor in New York, and the young Iranian hacker who had everything to gain by selling the handle on the open market in Iran. Through thousands of exchanged messages, misunderstandings, and the fits and starts of digital recovery, the story traces the intimacies—and stark asymmetries—produced by revolution, uprising, war, sanctions, state power, and censorship. 

 Salar Mameni will read from his daily “notes” written since the ongoing war on Iran began on February 28, 2026. In these notes, Mameni contemplates the politics of witnessing war and aggression from the diaspora, the divisions amongst the Iranian community and the collectivities formed in times of loss and violence. The dispersed nature of the diaspora pulls together in these notes through texting, facetime and brief moments of connectivity with Iranians experiencing continuous internet outages and digital blackouts.

 

Negar Mottahedeh is a Professor of Literature; Professor of Art, Art History & Visual Studies; Professor in Gender, Sexuality & Feminist Studies; and Professor of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies at Duke University. This fall (2026), Dr. Negar Mottahedeh has joined Stanford's Iranian Studies Program to teach a new course titled Iranian Visionary: On 'Abdu'l-Bahá's Modernism (GLOBAL 140). Her book #iranelection: Hashtag Solidarity and the Transformation of Online Life (Stanford University Press, 2015) examines the 2009 Iranian election protests and the emergence of social media as a platform for global political solidarity. The book traces how international activism around the #iranelection hashtag shaped the evolving online ecology of protest, anticipating practices such as hashtag activism, citizen journalism, avatar activism, and YouTube mashups. Her most recent book, Whisper Tapes: Kate Millett in Iran (Stanford University Press, 2019; Persian translation, Naakojaa Press, 2026), draws on Kate Millett’s archival recordings from the 1979 Iranian Revolution. It recovers the history of the women’s demonstrations that followed the revolution and explores the voices, slogans, experiences, and political imaginaries captured in Millett’s “whisper tapes.” Through a playful, alphabetically structured account, the book examines the Iranian women’s movement and the complex encounter between Western feminism and revolutionary Iran.

 

Salar Mameni is an artist, art historian and associate professor of comparative ethnic studies and affiliated faculty in the history of art department at UC Berkeley. He is the author of Terracene: A Crude Aesthetics (Duke University Press, 2023), which received outstanding achievement in Media, Performance, and Visual Studies from the Association for Asian American Studies in 2025 and honorable mention from the Association for the Study of the Arts of the Present in 2024. His second book Blood of Tulips is under contract with Duke University Press. Mameni’s essays have appeared in scholarly journals Representations, Qui Parle, Catalyst, Ramus, Resilience, Signs, Women & Performance, Critical Ethnic Studies, Visual Studies, Routledge Companion to Art, Visual Culture and Climate Change, and Al-Raida. His art criticism has been published in Canadian Art Journal, Fuse Magazine, and Fillip Review and in exhibition catalogues at the Third Line Gallery in Dubai, Mana gallery in Istanbul, and Sharjah Biennial. As an artist, Mameni has participated in numerous exhibitions with drawings in the collection of the Vancouver Art gallery and the Morris and Helen Belkin art gallery in Vancouver and has delivered lecture performances at Human Resources in Los Angeles, ProArts Gallery in Oakland, Goldsmiths college in London, the Listening Academy in London, and the Hemispheric Institute held in Mexico City among others.

event.title: Pediatric Grand Rounds (CME): Beyond Blood: Transplant and Gene-Edited Cell Therapy for Neurodegenerative Disease in Children
event.description:
Beyond Blood: Transplant and Gene-Edited Cell Therapy for Neurodegenerative Disease in Children


PRESENTER:
Natalia Gomez-Ospina, MD, PhD
Assistant Professor of Pediatrics, Medical Genetics
Stanford School of Medicine

 

SESSION DESCRIPTION
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is standard of care for a small number of neurodegenerative inherited disorders — metachromatic leukodystrophy, Krabbe disease, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and severe MPS type 1 — yet outcomes remain disappointing for most patients. Donor-derived cells repopulate the CNS slowly and incompletely, so neurologic decline often outpaces engraftment, while myeloablative conditioning and graft-versus-host disease impose morbidity that narrows the risk-benefit window. With newborn screening now detecting many of these disorders before symptom onset, the principal constraint on outcomes is no longer early diagnosis but the limitations of available therapy. This session reviews two developments that may substantially improve outcomes for these patients. The first is a conditioning strategy that pairs brain-penetrant chemotherapy with transient CSF1R inhibition, which in preclinical models achieves near-complete microglial replacement within weeks rather than months. The second is autologous transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells gene-edited at the CCR5 safe harbor to secrete supraphysiologic enzyme, eliminating the need for a matched donor and the risk of GVHD. Data will be presented across MPS type 1, Gaucher disease, and Friedreich’s ataxia, including evidence that engrafted myeloid cells benefit surrounding tissue not only through enzyme cross-correction but also by transferring intact mitochondria, with improvements in both neurologic and cardiac endpoints. The session closes with the manufacturing, genotoxicity, and regulatory requirements that stand between these results and first-in-human trials.

 

EDUCATION GOALS

  • Describe the current indications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in inherited neurodegenerative disease and the clinical factors — delayed CNS engraftment, conditioning-related toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease — that limit its benefit in rapidly progressive disorders.
  • Differentiate the mechanisms by which engrafted donor myeloid cells correct disease in the CNS and other tissues, and apply this understanding to anticipate which disorders and which patients are most likely to benefit.
  • Assess the preclinical efficacy and safety evidence for autologous hematopoietic stem cell products in lysosomal storage disorders, and identify their implications for patient counseling, timing of referral, and future trial eligibility.

event.title: Aging Wisely - Grief, Loss, and Legacy Making
event.description:
This class is co-sponsored by the Stanford WorkLife Office.

Caring for a terminally ill loved one or experiencing a sudden loss brings profound emotional challenges, often with little time to prepare. In this free webinar, we will explore best practices for navigating prolonged caregiving, being present at the end of life, and coping with sudden death.

Join us for a free webinar to offer tools and practices that can offer support as you experience grief and loss. We will discuss the immediate steps to take after a loved one’s passing, along with traditions and transitions related to burials, memorials, and rituals to honor the deceased. In addition, we will explore ways to honor your own grief process, including creative practices that use the arts to celebrate and preserve the legacies of those we love.

Through presentations and online discussions, you will learn strategies and tools to support yourself and others through grief and loss, while fostering meaningful ways to honor and remember loved ones.

event.description:
The Laurie J. Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce Dr. Mary Leonard as our Team Science Tuesday speaker for the Fall Quarter for a presentation titled “Team Science in Child Health Research: When the Whole is Greater than the Sum of the Parts.” We invite you to join us on Zoom on Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 11:00am. 

Mary B. Leonard, MD, MSCE is the Arline and Pete Harman Professor and Chair, Department of Pediatrics at Stanford University, Director of the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute (MCHRI), and Physician-in-Chief of Lucile Packard Children’s Hospital. Her research examines how chronic diseases—including kidney disease, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic conditions, and childhood cancer—impair bone and muscle development across the lifespan. Answering these questions requires partnership with colleagues in multiple pediatric subspecialties, as well as in biostatistics, epidemiology, anthropology, physics, engineering, and bioengineering, whose expertise underpins the advanced imaging and analytic methods central to her work. This collaborative model has allowed her to translate mechanistic findings into clinical trials and population-level studies while training investigators from many disciplines in patient-oriented research.

If you have any questions, please reach out to Nicole Foti (redacted@stanford.edu) or Daphne Martschenko (redacted@stanford.edu) .

event.title: Sustainable Systems Seminar Lunch Series -  Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models
event.description:
This week's speaker is:

Andreas Mühlbauer, Leavell Fellow and PhD student, Stanford University
"Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models"

Abstract:

Energy system models that plan highly renewable systems need high resolution in space and time. US grid operators schedule power in 15-minute intervals and dispatch real-time markets every 5 minutes. At such time steps, a full year of a large network quickly becomes too large to solve, so models are coarsened once and their error is rarely known. This talk presents a hierarchical approach similar to the nested grids of weather and climate models: a coarse model of the whole year and system is solved first, and its results serve as boundary conditions for finer levels that are solved in parallel time windows. We test the approach in PyPSA on standard IEEE networks with 14 to 118 buses, which are small enough to solve in full, so every gap to the optimum is exact. At 15-minute resolution, the hierarchy is 2.8–4.0 times faster on the same cores and stays within 0.45–0.9% of the optimum. I close with an outlook on bridging continental and local scales, using the example of zooming into US metropolitan areas.


Bio:

Andreas Mühlbauer is a Leavell Fellow and PhD student in Civil and Environmental Engineering at Stanford University, where he develops optimization frameworks for multi-sector energy systems. His research covers a range of topics in energy system transitions, including renewable integration, infrastructure planning, wind repowering, and carbon management. His current work focuses on renewable microgrids and on hierarchical methods for solving high-resolution energy system models.
Before Stanford, Andreas gained research experience at the Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology (Finland), the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (Germany), and the non-profit Energy Watch Group (Germany), working at the intersection of renewable energy modeling, carbon management technologies, and climate policy.

The topics of this seminar are broad but typically fall under technologies’ scaling potential and impact on (the system of) people, the environment and the economy. A particular focus is placed on the interaction potential of technologies with the energy, water, and material systems. Our goal is to create an intimate, collaborative space for students, postdocs, scientists, and PIs within Stanford across micro-level (material and technology) to macro-level (system) interests. These seminars will provide an opportunity to disseminate insights from your studies, connect with fellow researchers, and strengthen bonds across the community.

Dr. Pannu regularly briefs government officials and policymakers on emerging technologies with security implications, including artificial intelligence and synthetic biology.

event.title: Cross-National Comparison of Long-Term Care Fraud Oversight and Investigation Practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea
event.description:
As long-term care (LTC) services and public coverage expand, concerns about improper billing and fraudulent claims have also grown. These practices can divert public resources and place vulnerable beneficiaries at risk across LTC systems. In response, countries have developed approaches to identifying suspicious activities, investigating potential fraud, recovering improper payments, and imposing administrative, civil, or criminal consequences, reflecting the structure of their LTC systems and the types of misconduct they encounter. Although these systems differ across countries, cross-national comparison can reveal reciprocal policy and practice lessons regarding case triage, evidence development, interorganizational coordination, payment recovery, and enforcement. This study compares LTC fraud oversight and investigation practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea to identify transferable lessons for developing effective and sustainable fraud-control systems that preserve continuity of care for residents.

Speaker: Hyunkyung "Yulia" Yun, PhD, MS, MSW, is an Assistant Professor at the Herbert Wertheim School of Public Health and Human Longevity Science, UC San Diego. She earned her PhD in Health Services Research, specializing in health economics, at the Brown University School of Public Health. Her research evaluates health policies and care delivery systems affecting older adults, focusing on long-term care, managed care, and quality of care, using causal inference methods with claims, assessment, and EMR data. Previously, she worked at South Korea's National Health Insurance Service as a fraud investigator and researcher supporting the country's long-term care insurance system.

event.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Dr. Sarah Lambart  "From Basalt Chemistry to Mantle Mineralogy: Understanding Magmatism from Intraplate Volcanism to Continental Breakup"
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 320, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Abstract: Basaltic rocks provide a window into the Earth's mantle, recording information about the rocks that melt at depth and the processes that bring magma to the surface. But how much can we really learn about the mantle from basalt chemistry? In this seminar, I will first introduce BaSIC (Basalt Source Investigation and Characterization), a new open-source tool that uses the chemical composition of basalts to estimate the mineralogy of their mantle sources . Applying BaSIC to ocean island basalts reveals how tectonic setting and lithospheric thickness influence which mantle components contribute to melting. I will then show how we can use such tool to investigate the cause of magmatism during continental breakup, focusing on the opening of the Northeast Atlantic around 56 million years ago. Our results show that changes in mantle source mineralogy accompanied variations in magmatic activity, and suggest that thinning of the lithosphere, rather than high mantle temperatures alone, was a major driver of this magmatism.

event.title: L. Maria Bo, "Writing on Water: Cold War Literary Translations and the Chinese Diaspora," in conversation with Vaughn Rasberry
event.address: Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity (CCSRE), 450 Jane Stanford Way Building 360, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
During the Cold War, the ideological struggle to win the hearts and minds of the Chinese took place on the pages of literary texts. A battle of the books between Washington D.C. and Beijing mobilized entire networks of U.S. Foreign Service posts, book publishers, and higher education institutions to take sides in propagating representations of either democracy or communism to ethnic Chinese communities around the world. In Writing on Water, L. Maria Bo argues that these propagated literary texts, simply by undergoing translation, also became the means for new forms of anglophone Chinese identity and diasporic communities to emerge.

Rather than examining how translated literary texts produced strict equivalents that "worked" to spread ideology, Bo reads these texts as fluid equivocal exchanges. She attends to the various languages through which these texts traveled, including hegemonic varieties of English, numerous forms of Chinese, and other local patois. Doing so uncovers how ideology and meaning come undone in these texts-in-transit, allowing us imagine the formation of dispersed, ideologically diverse reading publics spanning East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the US heartland.

L. Maria Bo teaches classes in Asian, American, and Asian American literature. Her research is comparative, specializing in 20th/21st century literature between East Asia and the Americas. She studies translation to sound out fruitful crossings between critical translation theory, asian studies, and ethnic studies. Her first book focuses on English-Chinese literary translations during the Cold War to illuminate a methodology for studying multilingual diasporic literature. More recently, she has also begun to write on Asian/American science fictions.

Sponsored by the Research Institute of CCSRE.

event.title: Protest and Politics in Turkey in the 70s
event.description:
Protest and Politics in Turkey in the 1970s: Echoes of Dissent offers the first comprehensive academic study of Turkey’s protest cycle during the 1970s. Drawing on an original dataset, the book examines the interaction between collective action and state repression, tracing the development of leftist, nationalist, and Islamist movements throughout the decade. The book also analyzes how the 1980 military coup suppressed organized political activity and reshaped the political arena, contributing to the subsequent rise of political Islam and the country’s broader rightward shift. By connecting the political struggles of the 1970s to contemporary debates over authoritarianism, democracy, and protest, the study contributes to scholarship on social movements, repression, and political change.

This event is co-sponsored by CDDRL's Program on Turkey and the Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Selin Bengi Gümrükçü teaches political science at Rutgers University. She received her PhD from the University of Zurich. She previously taught at İzmir University of Economics and held visiting positions at Bielefeld University, Sciences Po, Paris 8, and the European University Institute. Her research focuses on social movements, political parties, the far right, political violence, and Europeanization, with an emphasis on Turkey. Her first book, Protest and Politics in Turkey in the 1970s: Echoes of Dissent, was published by Routledge in 2026.

event.description:
Join the Tech Impact and Policy Center on November 10th from 12PM–1PM Pacific for a seminar with Isabelle Hau.

Stanford affiliates are invited to join us at 11:40 AM for lunch, prior to the seminar. The Fall Seminar Series continues through December; see our Fall Seminar Series page for speakers and topics. Sign up for our newsletter for announcements.

About the Seminar:

As AI reshapes how we learn, work, and connect, understanding and strengthening human relationships has become an urgent scientific and societal priority. This session invites researchers across disciplines to explore Relational Intelligence (RQ), our capacity to build trust, cultivate belonging, navigate differences, and form meaningful connections. Together, we will examine emerging scientific questions, identify opportunities for interdisciplinary research, and imagine new ways to measure, develop, and strengthen relational capacities. How might we build a future in which advances in artificial intelligence are matched by advances in human connection?
 

About the Speaker:

Isabelle C. Hau is the executive director of the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, where she brings together learning & brain science, technology, and innovation to advance effective, inclusive, and human-centered approaches to learning.

Previously an impact investor, Isabelle led the U.S. education practice at Omidyar Network and Imaginable Futures, investing in mission-driven organizations that have reached millions of learners. She is the author of Love to Learn and a pioneer of Relational Intelligence (RQ), a framework for understanding and strengthening the human capacities to flourish in an age of AI.

Isabelle serves on the boards of Design Tech High School and EDC, as well as the EdSAFE AI Alliance steering committee, the Brookings Institution Global AI Taskforce, and the World Economic Forum’s Education 4.0 Alliance. Her honors include recognition by Harvard Business School as one of its 100 most inspiring women, being named a 2026 World Education Medal finalist, and receiving the 2026 ASU+GSV Power of Women Award and the 2026 ISTE/ASCD Impact Award. She has also been recognized for her contributions to early childhood education and human-centered AI. She once co-starred with Grover of Sesame Street.

Isabelle earned an MBA from Harvard Business School and graduated from ESSEC and Sciences Po Paris. Her lifelong professional goal is simple: to bring the love of learning to each and every child.

event.title: Applied Physics/Physics Colloquium: Dmitry Abanin - "Quantum advantage and computational complexity of many-body systems"
event.description:
Abstract: Quantum processors and simulators now probe the dynamics of hundreds of quantum constituents in regimes that challenge classical algorithms. These advances open unprecedented opportunities to explore quantum matter while raising a fundamental question: when do quantum simulations of many-body systems offer a meaningful computational advantage over classical methods? In this colloquium, I will describe recent experiments using superconducting analog and digital processors to prepare correlated low-energy states and probe their interacting quasiparticles. I will then discuss theoretical insights into the complexity of simulating many-body dynamics, showing how they inspire new classical algorithms while guiding the future applications of quantum processors.

Dmitry Abanin is Professor of Physics who joined the Princeton faculty in August of 2023. He received his Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2008. His scientific interests and areas of study include quantum simulation, quantum information and computing, condensed matter physics, and efficient classical algorithms for quantum systems. He has published over ninety peer-reviewed papers and has received numerous awards, including the recent Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher Award in 2023 and the ERC Consolidator Grant in 2020. He is currently on the graduate admissions committee for the new graduate program in Quantum Science and Engineering, which is a joint collaboration between the Physics and Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) Departments.

event.title: Science, Statecraft, and National Resilience: Rethinking Governance in the Philippines
event.description:
According to the World Risk Report 2026, the Philippines remained the world's most disaster-prone country among 193 United Nations member states. This is evident in the recent severe, frequent flooding that threatened lives, infrastructure, and economic stability. Climate change, rapid urban growth, deforestation, and poor planning have worsened flooding in the Philippines. To address this, the Philippines must adopt a proactive approach to disaster resilience, grounded in science-backed plans and decisions.

This presentation explores how scientific innovation and strategic policy intersect in the work of the University of the Philippines Resilience Institute (UPRI) and the Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards (NOAH) Center. By institutionalizing open data, high-resolution hazard mapping, and advanced predictive technologies, UPRI-NOAH bridges the gap between science and actionable policymaking. The

presentation highlights leading efforts to help government agencies and local communities integrate climate intelligence into governance frameworks and land-use planning. It demonstrates how positioning science as a pillar of statecraft can foster enduring national resilience by cultivating an adaptive society equipped to withstand environmental threats and safeguard the nation's future beyond the floodwaters.

This seminar is co-hosted by the Southeast Asia Program at Shorenstein APARC,  the Center for Sustainability in Southeast Asia at the Doerr School of Sustainability's Precourt Institute for Energy, and the Center for Human Rights and International Justice at Stanford Global Studies. Refreshments are sponsored by the Stanford Urban Resiliency Initiative.

Speaker

Dr. Alfredo Mahar Francisco A. Lagmay is a leading Filipino scientist in disaster risk reduction and climate resilience. An Academician of the National Academy of Science and Technology (NAST), UP Scientist III, and Professor at the National Institute of Geological Sciences, University of the Philippines, he leads two of the country’s flagship resilience institutions: the UP Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards (NOAH) Center and the UP Resilience Institute. Through these institutions, he has advanced real-time hazard monitoring, probabilistic risk assessment, open data systems, and science-based decision support for national and local governments.

His contributions to science and public service have earned national and international recognition, including the Plinius Medal of the European Geosciences Union (2015), the DOST Outstanding Research Award (2008), the PRC Outstanding Professional of the Year Award (2013), the Outstanding Filipino (TOFIL) Award (2013), the Start Network Changemaker Award (2020), the Office of Civil Defense Dangal ng Bantayog ng Katatagan Hall of Fame Award (2024), the UP Diliman Centennial Professorial Chair (2025), Tatler Asia’s Most Influential Philippines (2024, 2025), and the 2025 Tatler Impact Award for Innovation.

He earned his Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Geology from the University of the Philippines and completed his Ph.D. in Earth Sciences at the University of Cambridge.

event.title: A Rift in Time. Reinhart Koselleck and the Theory of History
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 200, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
What possible futures does history contain? Reinhart Koselleck has become one the most widely read and cited twentieth-century German historians and theorists of history, not just for the new field of “global conceptual history” but essentially for anyone across disciplines writing about questions of time, temporality, and historical thought. Yet the recent uptick of interest in his work as part of the “temporal turn” obscures the fact that Koselleck was working throughout his life on something even more ambitious: a new theory of history or rather a theory of the conditions of possible histories, and hence possible futures, written by an historian in an age of catastrophes.

Based on a wealth of previously inaccessible archival materials, this talk explores Koselleck’s critique of the modern concept of History and what he called its “temporalization”—from Critique and Crisis to his essays on dreams and war memorials—and parses out his parallel search for an antidote in the form of a new theory of historical knowledge, most visible in his late essay collection Sediments of Time. We will ask what remains of Koselleck’s theoretical reckoning with ruptured time and repetition in history and whether it can be untangled from the experiences of loss and complicity of his generation.

Join the Modern Europe Workshop in learning more about and discussing Stefan-Ludgwig Hoffman's research. RSVP for refreshments.

Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann is Chancellor’s Professor of History at the University of California, Berkeley. His most recent book, Der Riss in der Zeit. Kosellecks ungeschriebene Historik (Suhrkamp, 2023), will come out in English translation with Princeton UP in September 2027. Currently, he is working on two projects: a book-length essay on human rights internationalism from imperial beginnings to the present polycrises, and a monograph on everyday life in Berlin in the 1940s, as the city went from multinational capital of the Nazi Empire to shattered metropolis of the early Cold War. His previous two books traced the afterlives of Enlightenment concepts and social practices (sociability, humanity, cosmopolitanism, civil society) in the long nineteenth century and their late twentieth-century resurgence. Together with Samuel Moyn, he is the editor of the Cambridge series Human Rights in History.

What possible futures does history contain? Reinhart Koselleck has become one the most widely read and cited twentieth-century German historians and theorists of history, not just for the new field of “global conceptual history” but essentially for anyone across disciplines writing about questions of time, temporality, and historical thought. Yet the recent uptick of interest in his work as part of the “temporal turn” obscures the fact that Koselleck was working throughout his life on something even more ambitious: a new theory of history or rather a theory of the conditions of possible histories, and hence possible futures, written by an historian in an age of catastrophes.

Based on a wealth of previously inaccessible archival materials, this talk explores Koselleck’s critique of the modern concept of History and what he called its “temporalization”—from Critique and Crisis to his essays on dreams and war memorials—and parses out his parallel search for an antidote in the form of a new theory of historical knowledge, most visible in his late essay collection Sediments of Time. We will ask what remains of Koselleck’s theoretical reckoning with ruptured time and repetition in history and whether it can be untangled from the experiences of loss and complicity of his generation.

Join the Modern Europe Workshop in learning more about and discussing Stefan-Ludgwig Hoffman's research. RSVP for refreshments.

Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann is Chancellor’s Professor of History at the University of California, Berkeley. His most recent book, Der Riss in der Zeit. Kosellecks ungeschriebene Historik (Suhrkamp, 2023), will come out in English translation with Princeton UP in September 2027. Currently, he is working on two projects: a book-length essay on human rights internationalism from imperial beginnings to the present polycrises, and a monograph on everyday life in Berlin in the 1940s, as the city went from multinational capital of the Nazi Empire to shattered metropolis of the early Cold War. His previous two books traced the afterlives of Enlightenment concepts and social practices (sociability, humanity, cosmopolitanism, civil society) in the long nineteenth century and their late twentieth-century resurgence. Together with Samuel Moyn, he is the editor of the Cambridge series Human Rights in History.

event.title: Faculty Candidate Talk: “Candyman 5x: Playing Wretched in the Candyman Films of Bernard Rose and Nia DaCosta” | Zayla Crocker, PhD Candidate, UNC-Chapel Hill
event.description:
Situated in Black media studies and play studies, Zayla Crocker examines Bernard Rose’s 1992 film Candyman along with Nia DaCosta’s remake of the same name to demonstrate how both films encourage the spectator to “play” within the genre conventions of the slasher film through an act of ritualized play Crocker deems “playing wretched.” Both films overtly or covertly prompt the spectator to call on and summon the performance of Black memory, history, and trauma in the figure of a hook-handed slasher villain. As a whole, Crocker argues that the affective performance of horror and play acts as a memorial vehicle that situates the memory of Black trauma within the lived reality of the spectator. Outside of the film, spectators can join the game, and they too can call on Candyman and summon the memory of the other.

Zayla Crocker is a PhD Candidate and teaching fellow in the English Department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Her academic research focuses on the liberatory potential of the horror genre with an emphasis on media theory and cultural trauma through novels, films, and video games. Currently, her research is centered on Black expressions of trauma in the horror genre with a cross-media exploration of memory and affect.

event.title: Doing Development Differently: Lessons from BRAC on Local Leadership and Global Scale
event.description:
Foreign aid is declining amid overlapping global crises, placing significant pressure on the development sector. Rather than retreat or preserve approaches that no longer meet the moment, development leaders must rethink how change is funded and delivered, with greater emphasis on local leadership, strong systems, and collaboration rooted in the realities of the Global South.

The King Center on Global Development welcomes Asif Saleh, Executive Director of BRAC, one of the world’s largest development organizations, for a conversation on how global development is evolving with aid and philanthropy. Drawing on BRAC’s experience, Saleh will offer a practical, grounded perspective on how the sector can do development differently: shifting power closer to communities, building durable local capacity, and advancing solutions that can continue to deliver impact amid a changing aid landscape.

Dinner will be served.

About the speaker:

Asif Saleh is the executive director of BRAC, bringing leadership experience across the private, public, and nonprofit sectors with a track record of scaling development programs and building partnerships. He previously led strategy and communications at BRAC, spent 12 years at Goldman Sachs concluding as an executive director, worked as a policy specialist for UNDP Bangladesh, and led policy efforts on affordable broadband expansion and m-governance strategy as part of the Bangladesh Government’s national digital transformation initiative. Most recently, he was named to the 2026 TIME100 Philanthropy list.

event.title: Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis and Early Liver Transplantation
event.description:
Overview

This activity reviews the diagnosis and management of alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) and alcohol-associated hepatitis (AAH), including alcohol cessation strategies, treatment of alcohol use disorder, appropriate use of corticosteroids, and the evolving role of early liver transplantation. Learners will gain practical guidance on risk stratification, treatment thresholds, and timely referral of patients with severe alcohol-associated liver disease.

Registration

Registration for all practitioners - free.

To register for this activity, please click HERE

Credits

AMA PRA Category 1 Credits™ (1.00 hours), AAPA Category 1 CME credits (1.00 hours), ANCC Contact Hours (1.00 hours), Non-Physician Participation Credit (1.00 hours)

Target Audience
Specialties - Family Medicine & Community Health, Gastroenterology, Gastroenterology & Hepatology, Hematology, Internal Medicine
Professions - Advance Practice Nurse (APN), Non-Physician, Nurse, Physician, Physician Associate, Registered Nurse (RN)
 
Objectives
At the conclusion of this activity, learners should be able to:


1. Apply NIAAA clinical criteria and phosphatidylethanol testing to accurately diagnose alcohol-associated hepatitis and distinguish alcohol-associated liver disease from MASLD.
2. Use MELD rather than the Maddrey discriminant function to risk-stratify patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis and identify candidates for corticosteroid therapy.
3. Manage corticosteroid therapy appropriately, including assessment of contraindications and calculation of the Lille score at day 4 or 7 to discontinue treatment in non-responders.
4. Initiate concurrent treatment of alcohol use disorder using behavioral support and evidence-based pharmacotherapy, avoiding agents contraindicated in liver disease.
5. Identify patients appropriate for early liver transplant referral without applying a fixed 6-month sobriety interval, and document eligibility using specific, non-stigmatizing language.

event.title: Lunch Club Series | Beneath Tiahuanacu’s Streets: Ceramic iconography and Ancient Heritage in an Aymara town
event.description:
Lunch Club provides affiliates of the Stanford Archaeology Center with a community-oriented forum for engagement with current issues in archaeology. On Nov 11, 2026, we will host Dr.Paul Goldstein from University of California, San Diego.

Abstract:

Research on Tiwanaku ceramic iconography, including eclipse imagery and a little-known system of post-firing engravings, brought me to Tiahuanacu in 2026. Though long rumored to overlie an extension of the Tiwanaku UNESCO World Heritage site, the town was never systematically investigated until a 2024-25 salvage project for a new municipal sewer system. Directed by Tiahuanacu archaeologists, the project yielded significant finds that substantially add to and complement the Tiwanaku site museum’s collections. With funding from U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP), our project “Shared Heritage at Tiwanaku”, directed by Deborah Blom, Luis Callisaya and Hugo Avalos,  will work with Tiahuanacu archaeologists, excavation “maestros”, educators, tour guides, and local authorities to study the new finds and build inclusive educational materials and a new Municipal Gallery exhibit.

event.title: Mental Health Technology + Innovation Hubinar: Integrating AI into Virtual Reality for Mental Health Care (Panel)
event.description:
Join us on November 11th, 12-1pm PT for a panel on "Integrating AI into Virtual Reality for Mental Health Care".

Virtual and augmented reality are increasingly being used to deliver exposure-based treatments for anxiety related disorders, trauma, addiction, and other mental health conditions. Advances in artificial intelligence are now expanding what these technologies can do, enabling more interactive, adaptive, and personalized therapeutic experiences. In this panel, experts spanning clinical research and digital health will explore the evolving role of AI in virtual and augmented reality for mental health care. Panelists will share examples of AI-enabled tools designed to address real-world clinical needs, including interactive virtual characters, personalized exposure environments, and systems that can adapt treatment based on patient response. 

The discussion will examine where AI can meaningfully enhance therapeutic XR, what aspects of human interaction and real-world exposure these technologies are unable to replicate, and how clinicians can remain appropriately involved as systems become more adaptive. Panelists will also consider the guardrails needed for responsible use, the potential role of wearable data in personalization, and the practical challenges of moving promising tools from research and development into evidence-based clinical practice.

Panelists will share examples of AI-enabled tools designed to address real-world clinical needs, including interactive virtual characters, personalized exposure environments, and systems that can adapt treatment based on patient response. 

The discussion will examine where AI can meaningfully enhance therapeutic XR, what aspects of human interaction and real-world exposure these technologies are unable to replicate, and how clinicians can remain appropriately involved as systems become more adaptive. Panelists will also consider the guardrails needed for responsible use, the potential role of wearable data in personalization, and the practical challenges of moving promising tools from research and development into evidence-based clinical practice.

event.title: Negotiating Childhood: French Colonialism and African Children in Senegal - Kelly Duke Bryant
event.description:
How did French colonial institutions seek to define, regulate, and ‘‘protect’’ childhood in Senegal, and how did children respond?

In this talk based on her recent book, Negotiating Childhood: French Colonialism and African Children in Senegal, 1848–1940, Kelly Duke Bryant explores the lived realities of African children across courts, schools, streets, reformatories, vaccine clinics, and other sites of colonial intervention. Rather than treating children as passive subjects, Bryant illuminates the ways children limited or negotiated colonial reforms and how the colonial state’s reliance on cooperation produced unexpected forms of resistance and accommodation. The talk highlights long-term consequences of colonial governance, such as the privileging of chronological age and the centrality of official documentation, that continue to shape Senegalese childhoods.

Speaker Details

Kelly Duke Bryant is chair of the History Department at Rowan University, where she has taught since 2009. She earned her MA in history from the University of Wisconsin and her Ph.D., also in history, from Johns Hopkins University. A specialist in the history of West Africa, she has published scholarly articles and book chapters on the history of education, childhood, and youth in colonial Senegal. She is the author of two books, Education as Politics: Colonial Schooling and Political Debate in Senegal, 1850s-1914 (University of Wisconsin Press, 2015) and Negotiating Childhood: French Colonialism and African Children in Senegal, 1848-1940 (University of Massachusetts Press, 2026). She recently began a term as president of the French Colonial Historical Society.

Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Clive Neal  - "Why the Moon Needs an International Lunar Resource Prospecting Campaign"

event.description:
The Moon is a highly valued destination for human space exploration because it is close and it contains a wide array of lunar and Solar System science targets, which include resources that could be used to sustain humans on the lunar surface. These resources have the potential to enable sustainable human space exploration, develop a vibrant cislunar economy, and directly benefit society here on Earth. However, recent rhetoric about the importance and value of these resources has used the term as if we know they are reserves. An immediate and vital next step has not yet been realized to define the reserve potential of such resources, and that is designing and implementing a coordinated international lunar resource evaluation (prospecting) campaign. This talk discusses the issues that still need to be addressed by such a campaign, including why it needs to be international in nature and how the coordination can be started and evolved, as well as exploring the benefits that would come from prospecting on the Moon.

 

 

Clive R. Neal is a lunar evangelist and Professor of Planetary Geology at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, with 40 years of experience studying all aspects of the Moon and lunar exploration. He is passionate about establishing human permanence on the Moon in a way that benefits society here on Earth, while maximizing the scientific return that enables commercial involvement.

Neal has published over 150 peer-reviewed scientific articles and was a co-editor of the New Views of the Moon 1 and 2 volumes. He chaired NASA’s Lunar Exploration Analysis Group (LEAG) from 2006-2010, where he led the development of the U.S. Lunar Exploration Roadmap, and again from 2015-2018, when he formed the LEAG Commercial Advisory Board. In 2015, he received the NASA Wargo Award for the integration of exploration and planetary science throughout his career.

Neal was an advisor to the National Academies Committee on Astrobiology and Planetary Science (CAPS) from 2016 to 2017, and a member from 2018 to 2024. In 2019, he was invited to give testimony at the sixth meeting of the National Space Council regarding the importance of in-situ resource utilization. In 2025, Neal gave a technical presentation on lunar resource prospecting to the UN-COPUOS Legal Subcommittee; he gave another technical presentation to that subcommittee in 2026.

Also in 2026, Neal received two prestigious awards: NASA’s Eugene Shoemaker Distinguished Scientist Medal, which honors individuals who have made significant, career-spanning contributions to the field of lunar and planetary geoscience; and the AGU’s Waldo E. Smith Award, given biennially in even-numbered years to a senior scientist in recognition of extraordinary service to Earth and space science.

Currently, Neal is a member of the ESA Human-spaceflight and Exploration Science Advisory Committee (HESAC), a Steering Committee member of the NASEM study of Key Non-Polar Destinations Across the Moon, the co-chief editor of the new Space and Planetary Resources Journal, and a member of the Lunar Science Advisory Board for ispace-US.

Neal was educated in the UK, receiving his PhD from the University of Leeds. He moved to the U.S. in 1986, where he spent four years as a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Tennessee–Knoxville, studying Apollo samples. He joined the faculty at Notre Dame in 1990.

 

 

Speaker-suggested reading: Neal, C. R., et al. (2024). The Moon needs an international lunar resource prospecting campaign. Acta Astronautica, 214, 737–7.

event.title: Reimagining Democracy: America at 250
event.description:
As part of its free public programming, Stanford Continuing Studies is proud to present the third annual Reimagining Democracy, a weekly speaker series produced with the Office of Community Engagement, the Stanford Democracy Hub, and the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law.

This six-part series, hosted by Dean Debra Satz and Professor Larry Diamond, features Stanford scholars who help us understand democracy: how America’s founding 250 years ago shapes public life today, and where we go from here in reimagining and strengthening democratic values and governance, at home and around the world. This year’s series features constitutional, electoral, social science, and humanities experts with conversations connecting to the US November midterm elections and beyond. 

The series will be recorded and the videos will be available to view at a later date.

Schedule & Topics

October 7: Federalism in America 1776–2026

  • Jonathan Gienapp, Professor of History and Law and the Nehal and Jenny Fan Raj Civics Faculty Fellow in Undergraduate Teaching
  • Sarah Anzia, Senior Fellow (adjunct) at the Hoover Institution and Chancellor's Professor of Public Policy and Political Science at UC Berkeley

October 14: Global Democracy and Elections in Comparative Perspective

  • Alberto Díaz-Cayeros, Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and Co-Director of the Democracy Action Lab
  • Anna Grzymala-Busse, Michelle and Kevin Douglas Professor of International Studies and Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and, by courtesy, at the Hoover Institution

October 21: Money, Parties, and Politics

  • Brandice Canes-Wrone, Professor of Political Science, Maurice R. Greenberg Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, and Director of the Center for Revitalizing American Institutions
  • Didi Kuo, Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and manager of the Program on American Democracy in Comparative Perspective at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law

October 28: Voting Rights and Electoral Reforms

  • Nate Persily, James B. McClatchy Professor of Law at Stanford Law School and the Co-Director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative

November 4: Midterm Reflections

  • Ben Ginsberg, Volker Distinguished Visiting Fellow at the Hoover Institution
  • Pamela S. Karlan, Kenneth and Harle Montgomery Professor of Public Interest Law and Co-Director of the Supreme Court Litigation Clinic at Stanford Law School

November 11: Reimagining Civil and Public Service in Our Democracy

  • Joe Felter, Director of the Gordian Knot Center for National Security Innovation, Hoover Fellow, and retired US Army Ranger and Special Forces officer
  • Ira Lit, Professor, Graduate School of Education and Peter E. Haas Faculty Director of the Haas Center for Public Service
  • Lerone A. Martin, Martin Luther King, Jr., Centennial Professor in Religious Studies and Director of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute

event.title: Lauren Kolodny @ Entrepreneurial Thought Leaders Speaker Series (ETL)
event.address: 475 Via Ortega, Stanford, CA 94305, United States
event.description:
Lauren Kolodny is co-founder and managing partner of Acrew Capital, where she invests in companies transforming financial services through AI and technology. Her investment focus spans fintech, consumer technology, and enterprise software. Kolodny led Chime’s Series A in 2016 and supported the company at the board through its 2025 IPO. Her investments also include Alix, Bilt, Catena, Crux, Divvy (acquired by Bill.com), Gusto, Invisible Technologies, Plaid, and Wispr Flow. Before co-founding Acrew, Kolodny was a partner at Aspect Ventures. Previously, she worked in product marketing at Google, helping build Google Workspace and leading the launch of Google Drive. She began her career developing technology partnerships for the Clinton Foundation in India. She is a three-time Forbes Midas List honoree and was named to Barron’s 2026 list of the 100 Most Influential Women in U.S. Finance. She serves on the Stanford Graduate School of Business Trust and is a trustee emerita of Brown University.

This appearance by Lauren Kolodny is part of the Entrepreneurial Thought Leaders series. Subscribe to our eCorner YouTube channel, where we bring founders, investors and industry influencers to center stage and invite them to share what it takes to become a disruptor.
